first.rationale: Two declines are named in the situation (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) and only one slot exists, so the intervention should attack the shared upstream funnel rather than mask the competitor shock. memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value across self-serve) is the most directly on-target inherited belief and is the basis for the intended action. Verification triage: I spend the budget on the two beliefs that are simultaneously high-consequence and weakly supported *for the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue*, not on the belief I already intend to act on where the evidence is directionally aligned. (1) memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the loudest attractor this week because of the competitor's entry pricing, and it is recorded only as 'acquisition and revenue lift' \u2014 acquisition-volume and gross-revenue proxies that say nothing about margin, retention, or discount-cohort quality. If the archived record shows the lift was measured over a short window on discounted cohorts, pricing is disqualified for a long-term-revenue objective; if it shows durable retained revenue, it becomes a live contender and I should reconsider. That single pull has the highest chance of changing the decision. (2) memory_31 is the mechanism risk inside my own intended action: it attributes SMB activation lift specifically to *cutting required signup fields*. Fewer fields can raise activation counts while degrading lead qualification and routing \u2014 exactly the substitution of a proxy metric for qualified revenue that this objective forbids. I need to know whether the original record measured downstream qualified pipeline or only first-week activation before I let field-cutting into the design. It is also the oldest memory (day 12) and the most likely to have decayed. I deliberately do not verify memory_91 or memory_44: activation messaging is a weaker, more recent proxy-metric play, and enterprise sales-assist does not address either declining metric. Uncertainty preserved: all six memories are consolidated summaries with archived sources; none report qualified-revenue outcomes directly, so even the belief I am acting on is treated as directional rather than settled. Design consequences regardless of verification outcome: shorten and resequence onboarding steps rather than stripping qualification fields, instrument qualified-pipeline and 30/60-day retained revenue as primary readouts with completion and activation as secondary guardrails, and pre-register a stop rule if lead quality drops even while completion rises. If memory_73's record turns out to show durable retained revenue, I will re-rank promotional pricing for the next slot but would still run it as a small guarded test given margin exposure.

final.rationale: Both pulls paid off, and in opposite directions. exp_73 falsifies the loudest attractor: the 40% SMB discount bought signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% while burning 30-day retention -12%, and the original record explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. That cohort does not survive its first renewal, so promotional_pricing is disqualified against a long-term qualified-revenue objective no matter how sharp the competitor's entry pricing feels this week. The competitive shock is real but pricing is the wrong instrument for it; matching a discount war would trade durable revenue for a vanity acquisition spike. exp_31 survives verification with an important correction to my prior worry: cutting required signup fields cost only -1% on 30-day retention and still returned qualified revenue +4%, so the lead-qualification degradation I feared did not materialize at SMB scale. The recorded caveat is scope, not validity \u2014 'holds on SMB; not replicated on other segments.' So I proceed with simplify_onboarding, which attacks the one upstream mechanism shared by both declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) rather than masking the competitor shock with margin. Remaining uncertainty is now concentrated in the belief I did not verify: memory_86 is the load-bearing claim that shortening onboarding lifts completion and time-to-value across self-serve, and it remains an unverified consolidated summary reporting completion and adoption proxies, never qualified revenue. That is why this stays a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout, and why I scope it to SMB/self-serve where exp_31's evidence actually holds instead of extending to enterprise, where memory_44's sales-assisted path is the recorded pattern and my evidence does not transfer. Downstream value risk stands: completion rate and activation are proxies that can be inflated by removing friction that was doing qualification work. Design accordingly \u2014 shorten and resequence onboarding steps rather than stripping qualifying fields wholesale; make 30/60-day retained and qualified revenue the primary readouts with completion and activation strictly secondary; hold a clean control; pre-register a stop rule that halts if retention or lead quality degrades even while completion climbs, using exp_73's -12% retention as the cautionary shape to watch for. If results replicate memory_86's direction on revenue rather than just completion, that belief earns promotion from unverified summary to supported; if completion rises while qualified revenue is flat, treat it as a proxy win and do not scale it.
